title: 2-D and 3-D transformations and projection
kicker: ENCT 201 · Computer Graphics and Visualization · Chapter 3
subtitle: Moving, turning and scaling are just matrices. Combine them by multiplying, and watch the order.

sections.title: The basic 2-D transformations
sections.body:
Everything a graphics program does to a shape comes down to five moves. You can slide it: translate (x + tx, y + ty). You can stretch it: scale (sx·x, sy·y). You can spin it: rotate by θ about the origin (x cos θ − y sin θ, x sin θ + y cos θ). You can flip it: reflect (negate a coordinate). And you can lean it: shear (x + shx·y).

Each of these is a matrix, except translation in ordinary 2×2 form, and that awkward exception is exactly why graphics uses homogeneous coordinates (next section). First, try one: rotate the point (1, 0) by 90° about the origin. With cos 90° = 0 and sin 90° = 1, the answer is (0,1). The point has swung a quarter-turn counter-clockwise from the x-axis to the y-axis. Does that match your mental picture?

worked.why: Rotate the point (1, 0) by 90° about the origin.

questions.prompt: Rotating (1, 0) by 90° counter-clockwise about the origin gives…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The point moves up the y-axis.

keynotes: The five basic 2-D moves are translate, scale, rotate about the origin, reflect and shear.
Rotation by θ gives (x cos θ − y sin θ, x sin θ + y cos θ).
Rotating (1, 0) by 90° about the origin gives (0,1).

sections.title: Homogeneous coordinates and composition
sections.body:
Here is a beautiful trick to fix the awkward translation. Write a point as (x, y, 1), one extra coordinate, and suddenly every transformation, including translation, becomes a 3×3 matrix. One kind of object, one operation: multiply.

A sequence of transformations is then just the product of their matrices, applied right to left: M = Mₙ⋯M₂M₁ applies M₁ first. But matrix multiplication is not commutative, so order matters, and this trips up everyone once, so you should watch it closely. Test it: translate (2,3) then rotate 90° sends (1,0) to (-3,3), yet rotate first and then translate sends it to (2,4). Same two moves, different destinations. In the figure, the matrix on the right is the running product. Same result either way? No, certainly not.

questions.prompt: Translate (2,3) then rotate 90° versus rotate 90° then translate (2,3): same result?

choices.text: No — matrix multiplication is not commutative.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: They give (-3,3) and (2,4) for the point (1,0).

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Uniform scaling commutes with rotation, not translation.

keynotes: Writing a point as (x, y, 1) makes every transformation, including translation, a 3×3 matrix.
A sequence is the product of matrices applied right to left: M = Mₙ⋯M₂M₁ applies M₁ first.
Order matters: translate (2,3) then rotate 90° sends (1,0) to (-3,3), but rotate then translate sends it to (2,4).

sections.title: Rotation about an arbitrary point
sections.body:
Rotation about the origin is easy. But what if you want to spin a shape about its own centre, or any point you choose? There is a lovely sandwich recipe: translate the pivot to the origin, rotate, translate back. In matrices, T(px,py)·R(θ)·T(−px,−py).

Walk through it. Rotate (2,1) by 90° about (1,1). Translate so the pivot (1,1) is the origin: (2,1) → (1,0). Rotate 90°: (1,0) → (0,1). Translate back: (0,1) + (1,1) = (1,2). Scaling about a fixed point uses the very same sandwich. To rotate about a point other than the origin, you wrap the rotation between two translations.

worked.why: Translate so the pivot (1,1) is the origin: (2,1) → (1,0).

questions.prompt: To rotate about a point other than the origin you…

choices.text: Translate it to the origin, rotate, translate back.

figures.caption: Figure 3.3.1 — rotate about (1,1)
figures.note: The sandwich is applied for you.

keynotes: Rotation about a pivot (px, py) is T(px,py)·R(θ)·T(−px,−py): translate the pivot to the origin, rotate, translate back.
Scaling about a fixed point uses the same sandwich.

sections.title: Parallel and perspective projection
sections.body:
How do you squash a 3-D world onto a flat screen? There are two famous ways. In parallel projection the lines of projection are parallel: just drop z (orthographic). Sizes are preserved, which is why engineers use it in technical drawings. In perspective projection the lines converge at the eye: x′ = x·d/(d − z), so nearer things look bigger, just as railway lines meet at the horizon.

Try the maths. A cube vertex at z = −1 with eye distance d = 4 is scaled by 4/5, so (−1,−1) becomes -0.8,-0.8. Step through the figure to see the model, the rotated cube, the parallel and the perspective versions side by side. In perspective, distant objects appear smaller.

questions.prompt: In perspective projection distant objects appear…

choices.text: Smaller, because coordinates are divided by depth.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Parallel lines converge toward a vanishing point.

figures.caption: Figure 3.4.1 — a cube, two projections
figures.note: Step: model, rotated, parallel, perspective, side by side.

keynotes: Parallel projection drops z (orthographic): sizes are preserved, as in engineering drawing.
Perspective projection converges at the eye: x′ = x·d/(d − z), so nearer things look bigger.
A vertex at z = −1 with d = 4 is scaled by 4/5: (−1,−1) becomes (-0.8,-0.8).

sections.title: 3-D transformations
sections.body:
Add one more dimension and the story continues almost unchanged. You use 4×4 homogeneous matrices. Translation and scaling extend directly, and rotation is about an axis: Rz(θ) rotates x–y, Rx(θ) y–z, Ry(θ) z–x. Composite 3-D transformations are again products.

Try one: rotate (1,0,0) by 90° about the z-axis, giving (cos θ, sin θ, 0) = (0,1,0). One warning worth tattooing: rotations about different axes do not commute. Hold a book and turn it a quarter-turn about two different axes in both orders if you want to see this with your own hands.

questions.prompt: Do 3-D rotations about different axes commute?

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Same-axis rotations commute; different axes do not.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Rotate a book 90° about two axes in both orders and compare.

keynotes: 3-D uses 4×4 homogeneous matrices; rotation is about an axis: Rz(θ) rotates x–y, Rx(θ) y–z, Ry(θ) z–x.
Rotating (1,0,0) by 90° about the z-axis moves it to (0,1,0).
Rotations about different axes do not commute.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Three lines to carry out of this chapter.

  • Homogeneous matrices turn every transformation into a product.
  • M = Mₙ⋯M₁; order matters; pivot rotation = T·R·T⁻¹.
  • Parallel keeps size; perspective divides by depth.

If you can explain why order matters using the (1,0) example, you have understood the heart of it.
keynotes: Homogeneous matrices turn every transformation into a product.
M = Mₙ⋯M₁, order matters, and pivot rotation is T·R·T⁻¹.
Parallel projection keeps size; perspective divides by depth.
